documents.title: Yeshiva University Undergraduate AI Policy
tiers: UG 4: AI integrated into the assignment
documents.summary: The undergraduate colleges' policy sets a no-AI default unless the instructor allows use in writing, and gives instructors a five-level framework (UG 0 to UG 4) to state per course and assignment. It requires written disclosure above UG 0, treats undisclosed or out-of-level use as misconduct, and covers faculty AI use, data and IP, research, equity and review.
documents.stance_why: The document says "The colleges neither prohibit AI outright nor require it. Faculty decide how AI fits the learning goals of their courses," and offers a five-level tier framework "UG 0 through UG 4" that instructors choose per assignment, so under the tiers rule the stance is delegates even though the fallback is "the rule is no AI."

units.why: The Purpose section states that "preparing students for an AI-enabled world and protecting the integrity of their education are the same project," a framing principle of the whole policy, so it is an institution-level framework (P56) with an informs modality.
units.anchor: preparing students for an AI-enabled world and protecting the integrity of their education are the

units.why: "These policies are consistent with the broader policies of the University" ties this policy to existing university rules; P77 (comply with existing policy) fits better than P56 because it points to other policy rather than stating principles.
units.anchor: These policies are consistent with the broader policies of the University

units.why: "other forms of academic conduct and misconduct, such as plagiarism and cheating on examinations, continue to be governed by the University's existing academic integrity policies" says other misconduct stays under the existing integrity policy; this is P77 (existing policy governs), not P36, because it limits the policy's scope.
units.anchor: continue to be governed by the University's existing academic integrity policies

units.why: "The colleges neither prohibit AI outright nor require it" states the overall stance: no uniform ban or mandate, which leaves the decision to instructors; closest is P04, but it also rules out both extremes.
units.anchor: The colleges neither prohibit AI outright nor require it.
units.fit_note: Also says the colleges do not require AI and do not ban it outright, which P04 (instructor decides) does not state directly.

units.why: "Faculty decide how AI fits the learning goals of their courses" gives instructors the decision and ties it to learning goals; I chose P83 (align with learning objectives) over P04 because the sentence names the learning-goals criterion.
units.anchor: Faculty decide how AI fits the learning goals of their courses

units.why: The first design goal is to "give instructors clear authority and practical tools to set AI expectations for their own courses," which delegates the rule-setting to instructors (P04) and states it as a principle.
units.anchor: Give instructors clear authority and practical tools to set AI expectations

units.why: The goal "helping students build the AI skills their future careers will require" gives a professional-skills reason for permitting AI, so P44 (teach effective AI use as a professional skill).
units.anchor: helping students build the AI skills their future careers will require

units.why: "Develop responsible AI fluency appropriate to each discipline" sets AI literacy (using, verifying and taking responsibility) as a curricular aim, which matches P70 (AI-literacy training) more than P44 because it is about developing fluency, not employer expectations.
units.anchor: Develop responsible AI fluency appropriate to each discipline

units.why: "Protect intellectual property, safeguard student data privacy, and ensure equitable access to AI tools" lists three principles the policy pursues; it is a framework statement (P56) rather than a specific rule.
units.anchor: Protect intellectual property, safeguard student data privacy, and ensure equitable access to AI tools.

units.why: "when in doubt, don't; when unsure, ask" tells students to ask before acting under uncertainty, exactly P10.
units.anchor: when in doubt, don't; when unsure, ask.

units.why: "unless your professor tells you in writing that you may use AI on an assignment, you may not use it" bans AI unless the professor grants written permission; the key element is the written prior approval, so P107 over P06 (the fallback sentence is coded separately).
units.anchor: unless your professor tells you in writing that you may use AI on an assignment,

units.why: "Permission is never assumed. It is always granted, in writing, by your professor" says who grants permission and how (in writing, for a specific course or assignment), a prior-approval rule, P107.
units.anchor: Permission is never assumed. It is always granted, in writing, by your professor

units.why: "When no rule is stated, the rule is no AI" is the fallback when a syllabus is silent, exactly P06.
units.anchor: When no rule is stated, the rule is no AI.

units.why: "AI can strengthen those capacities or hollow them out, depending on how you use it" explains that AI use can undermine the capacities students come to build, so it is P41 (AI shortcuts practice that builds skill).
units.anchor: AI can strengthen those capacities or hollow them out, depending on how you use it.

units.why: "Work that AI does for you is potentially learning you did not do" gives the skill-building reason for limiting AI, P41.
units.anchor: Work that AI does for you is potentially learning you did not do.

units.why: "learning to use it well is part of preparing for your career" is the professional-skills argument for engaging with AI, so P44.
units.anchor: learning to use it well is part of preparing for your career

units.why: "Sometimes that means restricting it now so that you become a stronger thinker, and a better user of AI, later" justifies restriction as sequencing toward later skill, matching P08 (permission staged as skills develop) in spirit; I chose P41 since no staging mechanism is given.
units.anchor: restricting it now so that you become a stronger thinker, and a better user of

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Acceptable Use Policy
documents.summary: An IT policy for faculty and staff that supports responsible use of generative AI and sets conditions: no entering internal, restricted or personal data, checking accuracy and bias, disclosing AI-produced work, and no malicious content. It also covers research use, ethical guidance for instructors, vendor contracts, mandatory training, monitoring and a review cycle.
documents.stance_why: The policy "supports responsible experimentation with generative AI tools by its faculty and staff" and then sets conditions ("YU expects all YU faculty and staff to follow these guidelines"), so AI use is allowed with conditions, which is permit.

documents.title: Academic Integrity Policy: Resources (syllabus language)
documents.summary: A resources page from the academic integrity office offering four syllabus templates for AI (from assistive-only to none allowed) and tips on written assessments, detection and process evidence. It tells students that generative AI is not permitted in most classes unless the instructor says so.
documents.stance_why: The page gives faculty four syllabus templates ("Assistive Only", "Select Generative and All Assistive", "All Allowed", "None Allowed") and tells them to "adjust the templates as needed," so the decision is left to instructors; the tier-or-template rule makes the stance delegates.

units.anchor: in most classes, the use of generative artificial intelligence is not permitted
units.fit_note: Says 'most classes' prohibit, not all, so it describes a common default rather than a binding rule.

units.anchor: If explicit permission to use generative platforms has not been given by your instructor, you

units.anchor: You will need to cite your generative AI sources appropriately.

units.anchor: Citing Generative Artificial Intelligence in MLA

units.anchor: Faculty should make clear the expectations for academic integrity for their course.

units.anchor: Below are some recommended templates for syllabus language.

units.anchor: faculty should adjust the templates as needed to fit the educational goals of their course

units.why: The general template says "All assignments will be analyzed by Turn-it-in for plagiarism and AI use," a statement that a detection tool is used on all work, P40.
units.anchor: All assignments will be analyzed by Turn-it-in for plagiarism and AI use.

units.anchor: Evidence to the contrary will result in appropriate penalties

units.fit_note: The page offers four templates: Assistive Only, Select Generative and All Assistive, All Allowed, None Allowed.

notes: Doc 1 text has a placeholder effective date '[DATE]' and the title page says August 2026. Doc 2 is an IT policy for faculty and staff (internal document); its PDF text is one word per line and the properties table mislabels the title as an Incident Response Plan. Doc 3 is a wider resources page; Proctorio, electronic-exam logistics and time-management links were skipped as not about AI. Doc 3 template sentences that repeat across templates (e.g. the generative-AI ban) were coded once. Course layer deferred in the collect file. No new types proposed; UNCOVERED units: ask-safe-harbor and instructor duty to answer permission questions.
